optionExplanations: ✗ Scheduling a custom Lambda via EventBridge to rotate the password works but requires writing and maintaining the rotation code, which is significant operational overhead.
✗ The modify-db-instance CLI command only changes the password manually and provides no automated 30-day rotation, so it does not meet the rotation requirement.

✓ AWS Secrets Manager natively integrates with Amazon RDS to manage the master user password and automatically rotate it on a schedule (such as every 30 days) using managed rotation, with the least operational overhead.
✗ Systems Manager Parameter Store can store secrets but has no built-in automatic password rotation for RDS, so achieving 30-day rotation would require custom automation.

text: A company performs tests on an application that uses an Amazon DynamoDB table. The tests run for 4 hours once a week. The company knows how many read and write operations the application performs to the table each second during the tests. The company does not currently use DynamoDB for any other use case. A solutions architect needs to optimize the costs for the table. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: A. Choose on-demand mode. Update the read and write capacity units appropriately.
B. Choose provisioned mode. Update the read and write capacity units appropriately.
C. Purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity for a 1-year term.
D. Purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity for a 3-year term.
optionExplanations: ✗ On-demand mode does not use capacity units (you cannot set RCUs/WCUs), and it charges per request at a higher per-unit rate, which is more costly than provisioned mode for a known, predictable throughput; this option is internally contradictory and not the cheapest.

✓ Provisioned mode lets you set RCUs/WCUs to exactly match the known read/write rate during the 4-hour test, which is the most cost-effective choice for predictable throughput; capacity (or auto scaling) can be tuned around the weekly window.

✗ DynamoDB reserved capacity requires a 1-year commitment to a baseline of provisioned capacity running continuously, which is wasteful for only 4 hours of use per week and not justified for a single, infrequent test workload.
✗ DynamoDB reserved capacity for a 3-year term is an even longer commitment to continuous baseline capacity, making it the least appropriate option for sporadic weekly testing.

text: A company runs its applications on Amazon EC2 instances. The company performs periodic financial assessments of its AWS costs. The company recently identified unusual spending. The company needs a solution to prevent unusual spending. The solution must monitor costs and notify responsible stakeholders in the event of unusual spending. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: A. Use an AWS Budgets template to create a zero spend budget.
B. Create an AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitor in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console.
C. Create AWS Pricing Calculator estimates for the current running workload pricing details.
D. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor costs and to identify unusual spending.
optionExplanations: ✗ A zero spend budget alerts when any cost above zero is incurred, which is not a tool for detecting unusual spending patterns on an actively running EC2 workload and would just fire constantly.
✓ AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to monitor spend, automatically detect unusual cost spikes, and notify stakeholders, directly meeting the requirement.
✗ AWS Pricing Calculator only produces upfront cost estimates and does not monitor actual spend or send anomaly notifications.

✗ Amazon CloudWatch monitors operational metrics and can alarm on the published billing metric for a total threshold, but it does not intelligently detect unusual or anomalous spending patterns the way Cost Anomaly Detection does.

text: A marketing company receives a large amount of new clickstream data in Amazon S3 from a marketing campaign. The company needs to analyze the clickstream data in Amazon S3 quickly. Then the company needs to determine whether to process the data further in the data pipeline. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A. Create external tables in a Spark catalog. Configure jobs in AWS Glue to query the data.
B. Configure an AWS Glue crawler to crawl the data. Configure Amazon Athena to query the data.
C. Create external tables in a Hive metastore. Configure Spark jobs in Amazon EMR to query the data.
D. Configure an AWS Glue crawler to crawl the data. Configure Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics to use SQL to query the data.
optionExplanations: ✗ Creating external tables in a Spark catalog and running AWS Glue jobs requires writing and managing ETL/Spark jobs, which is more operational overhead than a serverless crawler-plus-Athena query approach.

✓ An AWS Glue crawler automatically infers the schema of the S3 clickstream data into the Data Catalog, and Amazon Athena then runs serverless SQL queries directly against S3, giving the fastest analysis with the least operational overhead.
✗ Setting up a Hive metastore and running Spark jobs on Amazon EMR requires provisioning and managing a cluster, which is high operational overhead.
✗ A Glue crawler is appropriate, but Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics is designed for streaming data, not for ad hoc querying of data at rest in S3, so it does not fit this batch S3 analysis use case.

text: A company runs an SMB file server in its data center. The file server stores large files that the company frequently accesses for up to 7 days after the file creation date. After 7 days, the company needs to be able to access the files with a maximum retrieval time of 24 hours. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: A. Use AWS DataSync to copy data that is older than 7 days from the SMB file server to AWS.
B. Create an Amazon S3 File Gateway to increase the company's storage space. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days.
C. Create an Amazon FSx File Gateway to increase the company's storage space. Create an Amazon S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data after 7 days.
D. Configure access to Amazon S3 for each user. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 7 days.
optionExplanations: ✗ DataSync copying only files older than 7 days does not address the need for a hot-access local cache for the first 7 days nor a 24-hour retrieval tier, and DataSync is for scheduled transfers, not ongoing SMB access plus tiering.

✓ An S3 File Gateway presents SMB/NFS access and caches frequently used files locally for fast access during the first 7 days, and an S3 Lifecycle rule transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days, whose standard retrieval (up to 12 hours, within the 24-hour requirement) meets the retrieval window cost-effectively.

✗ There is no 'Amazon FSx File Gateway' service; FSx File Gateway provides on-premises access to FSx for Windows File Server, not S3 Lifecycle tiering of objects, so the described configuration is invalid.

✗ Configuring direct S3 access for each user abandons the SMB protocol the company relies on and adds significant client reconfiguration; Glacier Flexible Retrieval also exceeds operational simplicity versus a File Gateway and changes the access pattern entirely.

text: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The application uses a database that runs on an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The application performs slowly when trafic increases. The database experiences a heavy read load during periods of high trafic. Which actions should a solutions architect take to resolve these performance issues? (Choose two.)
options: A. Turn on auto scaling for the DB instance.
B. Create a read replica for the DB instance. Configure the application to send read trafic to the read replica.
C. Convert the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Configure the application to send read trafic to the standby DB instance.
D. Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster. Configure the application to cache query results in the ElastiCache cluster.
E. Configure the Auto Scaling group subnets to ensure that the EC2 instances are provisioned in the same Availability Zone as the DB instance.
optionExplanations: ✗ Amazon RDS does not offer storage/compute auto scaling for read throughput on a single PostgreSQL instance in this way; storage autoscaling only grows disk and does not offload heavy read traffic.
✓ Creating a read replica and routing read traffic to it directly offloads the heavy read load from the primary, scaling read capacity and resolving the read-bound performance problem.
✗ A Multi-AZ standby is for failover only and cannot serve read traffic, so it does not relieve the read load.
✓ An ElastiCache cluster caches frequently accessed query results in memory, dramatically reducing repeated read load on the database during traffic spikes.
✗ Placing EC2 instances in the same AZ as the database reduces minor cross-AZ latency but does not address the database read-capacity bottleneck and harms resiliency.

text: A company uses Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes to run an application. The company creates one snapshot of each EBS volume every day to meet compliance requirements. The company wants to implement an architecture that prevents the accidental deletion of EBS volume snapshots. The solution must not change the administrative rights of the storage administrator user. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative effort?
options: A. Create an IAM role that has permission to delete snapshots. Attach the role to a new EC2 instance. Use the AWS CLI from the new EC2 instance to delete snapshots.
B. Create an IAM policy that denies snapshot deletion. Attach the policy to the storage administrator user.
C. Add tags to the snapshots. Create retention rules in Recycle Bin for EBS snapshots that have the tags.
D. Lock the EBS snapshots to prevent deletion.
optionExplanations: ✗ Creating an IAM role on a separate EC2 instance to perform deletions does nothing to prevent accidental deletion and adds operational complexity; it does not protect snapshots.
✗ An IAM deny policy attached to the storage administrator user would change/restrict that user's administrative rights, which the requirement explicitly forbids.

✓ Amazon EBS snapshots placed in Recycle Bin via tag-based retention rules are recoverable after accidental deletion without altering the admin's permissions; configured once, this is the least-effort solution and is AWS's recommended approach for accidental-deletion protection.

✗ Snapshot Lock enforces WORM/immutability and would prevent the storage administrator from deleting snapshots at all, effectively changing what the admin can do, and locking each daily snapshot is higher administrative effort.

text: A company's application uses Network Load Balancers, Auto Scaling groups, Amazon EC2 instances, and databases that are deployed in an Amazon VPC. The company wants to capture information about trafic to and from the network interfaces in near real time in its Amazon VPC. The company wants to send the information to Amazon OpenSearch Service for analysis. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: A. Create a log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the log group. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the logs from the log group to OpenSearch Service.

B. Create a log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the log group. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the logs from the log group to OpenSearch Service.
C. Create a trail in AWS CloudTrail. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the trail. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the logs from the trail to OpenSearch Service.
D. Create a trail in AWS CloudTrail. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the trail. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the logs from the trail to OpenSearch Service.
optionExplanations: ✗ VPC Flow Logs can be sent to a CloudWatch Logs log group, but Kinesis Data Streams does not natively deliver to OpenSearch Service without custom consumer code/Lambda, adding operational overhead, so this is not the best fit.

✓ VPC Flow Logs are delivered to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter can stream the data to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, which has a built-in, fully managed delivery integration to Amazon OpenSearch Service in near real time with no custom code.
✗ AWS CloudTrail records API/management events, not network interface traffic; VPC Flow Logs cannot be sent to a CloudTrail trail, so this configuration is invalid.

✗ AWS CloudTrail captures API activity, not VPC network traffic, and VPC Flow Logs cannot target a CloudTrail trail, so even though Firehose can deliver to OpenSearch, the source configuration is invalid.

text: A company is developing an application that will run on a production Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The EKS cluster has managed node groups that are provisioned with On-Demand Instances. The company needs a dedicated EKS cluster for development work. The company will use the development cluster infrequently to test the resiliency of the application. The EKS cluster must manage all the nodes. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: A. Create a managed node group that contains only Spot Instances.
B. Create two managed node groups. Provision one node group with On-Demand Instances. Provision the second node group with Spot Instances.
C. Create an Auto Scaling group that has a launch configuration that uses Spot Instances. Configure the user data to add the nodes to the EKS cluster.
D. Create a managed node group that contains only On-Demand Instances.
optionExplanations: ✓ An EKS managed node group with only Spot Instances is the cheapest option, lets EKS manage all nodes, and Spot interruptions suit an infrequent dev cluster used to test application resiliency.
✗ Two managed node groups (On-Demand plus Spot) adds the higher cost of On-Demand capacity that an infrequent dev/test cluster does not need, so it is not the most cost-effective.

✗ A self-managed EC2 Auto Scaling group with a launch configuration that joins nodes via user data is not managed by EKS, violating the requirement that EKS manage all nodes (launch configurations are also legacy).
✗ A managed node group with only On-Demand Instances is the most expensive choice and is not cost-effective for an infrequently used development cluster.

text: A company stores sensitive data in Amazon S3. A solutions architect needs to create an encryption solution. The company needs to fully control the ability of users to create, rotate, and disable encryption keys with minimal effort for any data that must be encrypted. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: A. Use default server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3) to store the sensitive data.
B. Create a customer managed key by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Use the new key to encrypt the S3 objects by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).
C. Create an AWS managed key by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Use the new key to encrypt the S3 objects by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).
D. Download S3 objects to an Amazon EC2 instance. Encrypt the objects by using customer managed keys. Upload the encrypted objects back into Amazon S3.
optionExplanations: ✗ SSE-S3 uses Amazon-managed keys that customers cannot create, rotate on demand, or disable, so it fails the full key-control requirement.
✓ A customer managed KMS key used with SSE-KMS gives the company full control to create, rotate, and disable the encryption key with minimal effort, exactly meeting the requirement.
✗ An AWS managed KMS key does not allow customers to manage rotation, disable, or fully control its lifecycle, so it does not meet the control requirement.
✗ Manually downloading, encrypting on EC2, and re-uploading objects is high-effort, error-prone client-side encryption that contradicts the minimal-effort requirement.

text: A company wants to back up its on-premises virtual machines (VMs) to AWS. The company's backup solution exports on-premises backups to an Amazon S3 bucket as objects. The S3 backups must be retained for 30 days and must be automatically deleted after 30 days. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)
options: A. Create an S3 bucket that has S3 Object Lock enabled.
B. Create an S3 bucket that has object versioning enabled.
C. Configure a default retention period of 30 days for the objects.
D. Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to protect the objects for 30 days.
E. Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to expire the objects after 30 days.
F. Configure the backup solution to tag the objects with a 30-day retention period
optionExplanations: ✓ Creating an S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock enabled provides WORM (write-once-read-many) immutability so backups cannot be deleted or overwritten during the retention window; this is the foundation for the 30-day retention requirement.

✗ While S3 Object Lock technically requires versioning, enabling Object Lock at bucket creation automatically enables versioning, so separately configuring versioning is redundant and not one of the three required distinct steps.

✓ Configuring a default Object Lock retention period of 30 days enforces that every object is automatically protected (immutable) for 30 days without the backup solution having to specify it per object.
✗ An S3 Lifecycle policy does not 'protect' or lock objects; lifecycle rules only transition or expire objects, so this option does not achieve immutability and is incorrect.
✓ An S3 Lifecycle policy configured to expire objects after 30 days automatically deletes them once the 30-day period elapses, satisfying the automatic-deletion requirement.
✗ Tagging objects with a '30-day retention period' tag has no enforcement effect on its own; tags do not lock objects or delete them, so this does not meet the requirement.

text: A solutions architect needs to copy files from an Amazon S3 bucket to an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system and another S3 bucket. The files must be copied continuously. New files are added to the original S3 bucket consistently. The copied files should be overwritten only if the source file changes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A. Create an AWS DataSync location for both the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Create a task for the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Set the transfer mode to transfer only data that has changed.

B. Create an AWS Lambda function. Mount the file system to the function. Set up an S3 event notification to invoke the function when files are created and changed in Amazon S3. Configure the function to copy files to the file system and the destination S3 bucket.

C. Create an AWS DataSync location for both the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Create a task for the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Set the transfer mode to transfer all data.

D. Launch an Amazon EC2 instance in the same VPC as the file system. Mount the file system. Create a script to routinely synchronize all objects that changed in the origin S3 bucket to the destination S3 bucket and the mounted file system.
optionExplanations: ✓ AWS DataSync with locations for the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system, scheduled tasks, and transfer mode set to transfer only data that changed continuously copies new/changed files while overwriting only when the source changes, all as a managed service with the least operational overhead.

✗ A Lambda function with a mounted EFS file system and S3 event notifications works but requires writing and maintaining custom code, packaging, and error handling, which is more operational overhead than DataSync.

✗ DataSync is the right service, but setting transfer mode to transfer all data re-copies everything each run rather than only changed files, violating the overwrite-only-if-changed requirement and wasting transfer.
✗ A self-managed EC2 instance with custom sync scripts and a mounted file system carries the most operational overhead for patching, scripting, and scheduling.

text: A company uses Amazon EC2 instances and stores data on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. The company must ensure that all data is encrypted at rest by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). The company must be able to control rotation of the encryption keys. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A. Create a customer managed key. Use the key to encrypt the EBS volumes.
B. Use an AWS managed key to encrypt the EBS volumes. Use the key to configure automatic key rotation.
C. Create an external KMS key with imported key material. Use the key to encrypt the EBS volumes.
D. Use an AWS owned key to encrypt the EBS volumes.
optionExplanations: ✓ A customer managed KMS key lets the company control key rotation (and other key policies) while encrypting EBS volumes, meeting the requirement with the least operational overhead.
✗ An AWS managed key only supports AWS-controlled automatic rotation; customers cannot control its rotation, so it fails the control requirement.
✗ An external KMS key with imported key material gives control but adds substantial operational overhead to import, track expiration, and re-import material, which is more effort than needed.
✗ An AWS owned key is not visible or controllable by the customer at all and cannot satisfy the customer-controlled rotation requirement.

text: A company needs a solution to enforce data encryption at rest on Amazon EC2 instances. The solution must automatically identify noncompliant resources and enforce compliance policies on findings. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
options: A. Use an IAM policy that allows users to create only encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Use AWS Config and AWS Systems Manager to automate the detection and remediation of unencrypted EBS volumes.

B. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to manage access to encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Use AWS Lambda and Amazon EventBridge to automate the detection and remediation of unencrypted EBS volumes.
C. Use Amazon Macie to detect unencrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Use AWS Systems Manager Automation rules to automatically encrypt existing and new EBS volumes.
D. Use Amazon inspector to detect unencrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Use AWS Systems Manager Automation rules to automatically encrypt existing and new EBS volumes.
optionExplanations: ✓ An IAM policy permitting only encrypted EBS volume creation plus AWS Config rules with AWS Systems Manager automation to detect and remediate unencrypted volumes provides automatic identification of noncompliant resources and enforced remediation with the least administrative overhead.
✗ Using KMS to manage key access with custom Lambda and EventBridge automation requires building and maintaining custom detection/remediation code, which is more administrative overhead.
✗ Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it does not detect unencrypted EBS volumes, so this option is technically wrong.
✗ Amazon Inspector assesses software vulnerabilities and network exposure, not EBS volume encryption status, so it cannot detect unencrypted EBS volumes.

text: A company is migrating its multi-tier on-premises application to AWS. The application consists of a single-node MySQL database and a multi-node web tier. The company must minimize changes to the application during the migration. The company wants to improve application resiliency after the migration. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: A. Migrate the web tier to Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer.
B. Migrate the database to Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind a Network Load Balancer.
C. Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment.
D. Migrate the web tier to an AWS Lambda function.
E. Migrate the database to an Amazon DynamoDB table.
optionExplanations: ✓ Moving the web tier to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer preserves the existing multi-node web application with minimal change while adding elasticity and resiliency.

✗ Running MySQL on self-managed EC2 in an Auto Scaling group behind a Network Load Balancer is not a valid relational database HA pattern and adds operational complexity rather than improving resiliency simply.
✓ Migrating the database to Amazon RDS MySQL Multi-AZ keeps the MySQL engine (minimal application change) while adding synchronous standby failover for improved resiliency.
✗ Rewriting the web tier as AWS Lambda is a significant application re-architecture, conflicting with the minimize-changes requirement.
✗ Migrating to DynamoDB requires rewriting the data model and queries away from MySQL, a major change that violates the minimize-changes requirement.

text: A company wants to migrate its web applications from on premises to AWS. The company is located close to the eu-central-1 Region. Because of regulations, the company cannot launch some of its applications in eu-central-1. The company wants to achieve single-digit millisecond latency. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: A. Deploy the applications in eu-central-1. Extend the company’s VPC from eu-central-1 to an edge location in Amazon CloudFront.
B. Deploy the applications in AWS Local Zones by extending the company's VPC from eu-central-1 to the chosen Local Zone.
C. Deploy the applications in eu-central-1. Extend the company’s VPC from eu-central-1 to the regional edge caches in Amazon CloudFront.
D. Deploy the applications in AWS Wavelength Zones by extending the company’s VPC from eu-central-1 to the chosen Wavelength Zone.
optionExplanations: ✗ Extending a VPC to a CloudFront edge location is not how CloudFront works (it caches content, not VPC subnets) and does not let you run application compute outside the Region, so it cannot meet the regulatory and latency needs.

✓ AWS Local Zones extend the eu-central-1 VPC to a metro location closer to users but outside the Region proper, allowing the restricted applications to run with single-digit millisecond latency while complying with the not-in-eu-central-1 constraint.
✗ CloudFront regional edge caches are an internal caching layer you cannot deploy applications into or extend a VPC to, so this does not satisfy the requirements.
✗ AWS Wavelength Zones are designed for ultra-low-latency access over 5G mobile carrier networks, not general web application deployment for nearby data-center users, making it the wrong fit here.
